Meeting Header:
Date: 2025-08-05
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~58m
Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Marco (Redwood Infra SE); Jasmine, Rohit, Elena, Samir (AtlasPay)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be incomplete):
Quick deep-dive on throughput tuning for AtlasPay's on-prem/private deployment. Covered continuous batching behavior, scheduler knobs (max_num_seqs, token guards, priority lanes), KV cache hit dynamics, quantization tradeoffs, and VPC/on-prem networking constraints. Agreed to run a short on-prem smoke benchmark and exchange knob defaults + traffic profile.

Topics: continuous batching, max_num_seqs, token limits, slot stealing, kv cache eviction, quantization implications, VPC throughput, on-prem burst capacity

Transcript Body:
[00:00] Alex: hey everyone thanks for joining, um let's do a quick round of intros then jump into the perf bits, we have about an hour
[00:10] Jasmine: thanks Alex, Jasmine here, we own ML infra at AtlasPay and we're trying to get predictable 99th percentile latency for transactional chat flows
[00:18] Rohit: Rohit, platform, i'll be running the bench and provisioning nodes
[00:23] Alex: great, Priya and Marco from our infra team will cover scheduler knobs and kv-cache behavior
[00:28] Priya: hi all, i'll start by sketching the high-level problem: you've got bursty transactional traffic, lots of short seqs (10-60 tokens) but occasional long requests 500-1k tokens, and you want to maximize throughput while keeping p99 under 350ms if possible
[00:45] Samir: right we can't sacrifice cost too much, but outages are worse than cost spikes, so predictable latency is priority
[00:53] Priya: got it. ok, continuous batching in our runtime tries to fill batches opportunistically by waiting a tiny window until a batch is full or a latency deadline hits. two knobs we care about: max_num_seqs (per-GPU active sequence cap) and slot allocation policies - these control effective parallelism
[01:20] Priya: the tricky bit is short vs long seqs. if you set max_num_seqs too high you'll have many sequences active and KV cache strain, cache thrash, and longer tail; too low and you underutilize GPU and throughput drops
[01:40] Marco: and there's also token-level guards: per-request token_limit and bucket rate guards. We expose soft_limit (which triggers early batching windows) and hard_cap which will reject or fallback when exceeded
[02:05] Jasmine: can you explain slot stealing? we saw that term in the doc but not sure how it affects p99
[02:12] Priya: yeah slot stealing is an internal optimization where high-priority lanes can preempt lower-priority slots when a burst arrives. it's great for low-latency customers but can reduce fairness and increase retry rates for background workloads
[02:30] Rohit: so is priority lane basically reserved slots per-tenant? will that require dedicated capacity?
[02:36] Marco: you can configure priority lanes as soft reservations — e.g., reserve N slots but allow burst using slot stealing up to a burst_capacity. doesn't require full dedicated cluster but you need to tune max_num_seqs and burst_capacity together
[02:55] Priya: example: if gpu has max_num_seqs=64 and priority_reserve=8 with burst_capacity=16, we'll try to keep 8 slots available for priority, but allow up to 16 borrowed in short bursts. after that we hit token_hard_cap and either queue or fallback to a cheaper model
[03:20] Jasmine: fallback to a cheaper model is appealing for cost but worried about semantic regressions
[03:26] Alex: that's where our canary/fallback policy comes in — you can define per-route quality thresholds and automatic re-route on degradation, also include eval prompts to detect meaningful regressions
[03:36] Rohit: on the KV cache piece, what eviction strategy do you use? LRU? TTL? we saw bad hit rates in earlier runs
[03:43] Marco: we use an LRU-ish approach with hotness boosting for shorter sequences. There's a cold-start epoch for new model versions where KV cache warms slowly; we recommend a pre-warm phase for on-prem rollouts. Also you can pin prefixes for high-value flows
[04:02] Priya: important nuance — KV cache hitrate is not monotonic with max_num_seqs. Increasing parallel sequences can dilute per-seq cache locality, so hitrate goes down and per-token compute rises
[04:18] Jasmine: that aligns with our observations — when we ramp concurrency we saw p50 drop but p99 jump
[04:23] Priya: yep that's the signature of cache thrash. Some knobs to tune: reduce max_num_seqs, increase per-tenant slot affinity (keep sequences from same customer on same GPU where possible), and tune continuousBatch.window_ms smaller for short seq heavy workloads
[04:45] Rohit: for window_ms do you have recommended values? we've been using defaults and not sure where to start
[04:49] Priya: for short-seq heavy transactional apps we often go window_ms=8-12ms with max_num_seqs around 32-48 on A100-like cards. For mixed workloads bump window to 20-30ms and increase max_num_seqs to 64-96 to smooth long seqs
[05:10] Samir: do these numbers change drastically when you quantize models? we're considering int8 to halve memory and maybe increase batch sizes
[05:18] Marco: quantization reduces memory and can increase throughput, but it can also change per-token latency due to different kernel performance. With int8 we usually can increase max_num_seqs by ~1.5x safely, but watch quantization-induced quality drift for prompts with numeric or specialized tokens
[05:35] Priya: also kv cache representation changes for quantized kernels; hit penalty may differ, so run your workload with representative prompts in the bench to measure real impact
[05:46] Jasmine: ok. networking — we're running in our VPC on prem, we plan to peer. Any gotchas for token ingress/egress cost or socket timeouts causing long tails?
[05:56] Marco: on-prem VPC peering is fine, but watch for small packet delays — our runtime favors sticky connections and multiplexed streams. Timeouts should be tuned higher for long-generation flows (set request_timeout > expected max tokens * per-token ms). For short flows keep the request timeout tight to avoid stale hanging inflight requests
[06:18] Rohit: what's the recommended request_timeout for 1k-token worst-case?
[06:21] Priya: base estimate: per-token 6-12ms depending on model/quantization. For 1k tokens set request_timeout to 12s–18s as an upper bound during bench, then observe tail. But prefer streaming partial responses to avoid client-side timeouts
[06:40] Jasmine: streaming helps user experience but complicates billing and batching right?
[06:44] Priya: yes streaming reduces batchability because we flush tokens earlier. It's a tradeoff: streaming for user-facing low-latency partials, batched for throughput. We have hybrid strategies: enable streaming after first N tokens or on priority lanes only
[06:59] Samir: about guardrails — token_limit per-request, do you support dynamic token caps per-tenant? we want to cap third-party integrations but allow internal flows higher limits
[07:10] Marco: yes, token_limit can be configured per-route or per-API-key. We also expose a token_bucket_rate which limits sustained tokens/sec and a burst allowance that decays. Useful for preventing noisy neighbors from starving the KV cache
[07:27] Rohit: will the token bucket interfere with continuous batching? like will small token budgets cause spiky scheduling?
[07:32] Priya: it can. If token budget is exhausted, requests will be queued or rejected, which reduces batch fullness. Best practice: set token_bucket_rate to match expected steady-state throughput and rely on priority lanes for occasional spikes rather than aggressive bucket limits
[07:48] Jasmine: can you show the demo config for adaptive slots?
[07:52] Priya: sure I have a sample. (screen-share sounds) config snippet:
- max_num_seqs: 48
- continuousBatch.window_ms: 10
- priority_reserve: 6
- burst_capacity: 12
- token_hard_cap: 2000
- token_bucket_rate: 1200 tokens/sec
- kv_cache_eviction: lru_boosted
- fallback_model: llama-medium-quant

[08:28] Priya: note fallback_model is the model we route to when hard caps hit; keep fallback of similar quality or run quick eval set to detect regression
[08:36] Samir: curious about autoscaling — do you recommend horizontal scale vs increasing max_num_seqs per GPU?
[08:43] Marco: horizontal scaling (more GPUs) gives isolation and reduces interference at cost of orchestration. Increasing max_num_seqs is cheap but risks KV thrash and headroom loss. For predictable p99 we prefer bounded max_num_seqs + autoscale groups with per-tenant affinity
[09:02] Rohit: affinity would keep a tenant's sequences on same GPU? what about multi-tenant fair share?
[09:09] Priya: we do soft-affinity: try to colocate sequences for better cache locality, but enforce fairness via priority lanes and per-tenant token budgets. If a single tenant spikes, slot stealing allows priority traffic to preempt according to policy
[09:25] Jasmine: what about canarying a new max_num_seqs value? we want to test max=96 but don't want global risk
[09:31] Alex: use rollout policies — canary traffic (1-5%) with metrics gating on p50/p95/p99 and kv_cache_hitrate. We also have automatic rollback if p99 increases by X% or kv hit drops below threshold
[09:42] Rohit: what metrics should we capture during bench run?
[09:45] Priya: capture per-GPU CPU/GPU utilization, free memory, kv_cache_hitrate, per-request seq length distribution, batch fullness, tokens/sec, p50/p95/p99 latency, and queue depth histograms. Also keep error/retry counts
[09:58] Samir: ok makes sense. can you explain queue depth histograms?
[10:02] Priya: it shows how many requests wait before being batched. If you see spikes at high queue depth it indicates backpressure and you might need more capacity or tighter token limits
[10:12] Jasmine: we observed an odd behavior where p99 jumps when we enable streaming for a subset of routes — is that expected?
[10:19] Marco: yes streaming can cause partial flushes, making some batches smaller but earlier. If priority streaming routes preempt, they can fragment batches for other routes leading to higher tail. Consider dedicating streaming to priority lanes or using hybrid strategy
[10:34] Rohit: any recommended knob combos for on-prem GPUs (4xA100 per rack) with mostly short seq load?
[10:40] Priya: for that topology start with: max_num_seqs 40, window_ms 10, priority_reserve 4, burst_capacity 8, token_bucket_rate tuned to expected concurrent tokens, kv pinning for top 10 prefixes. Run 30-minute bench and iterate
[10:56] Samir: about prefix pinning — how do we pin and for how long?
[11:00] Marco: you can call the cache API to pin prefixes for a TTL or until eviction pressure. Pin only small high-value prefixes. Excessive pinning reduces effective cache capacity and can harm others
[11:11] Jasmine: any thoughts on observability — how to surface kv_cache thrash quickly?
[11:16] Priya: compute kv_hitrate over sliding windows and correlate with batch fullness and p99. We have dashboards with heatmaps of kv_hitrate per-GPU and per-route; set alerts if kv_hitrate drops by 20% from baseline
[11:28] Rohit: for our on-prem, we'll need the config file and a sample helm/ansible snippet to set these knobs, can you provide?
[11:36] Alex: yes we'll send that as part of the cheat sheet. Priya will include helm values, Marco will include notes on kernel/quant settings
[11:45] Samir: good. one more question — if we increase max_num_seqs but keep token_hard_cap low, will that protect us from long-seq storms?
[11:52] Priya: token_hard_cap helps but can lead to request rejection for valid long flows. Better combined approach: enforce per-route token limits, use fallback models for very long requests, and set per-tenant bucket rates. This keeps latency stable while allowing long jobs on lower-priority lanes
[12:10] Rohit: about error modes — do you provide automatic reroute to hosted if on-prem node is saturated?
[12:15] Marco: yes if you enable hybrid routing we can failover to hosted or dedicated pool; it's configurable policy: failover only on capacity vs on errors. For outages you can prefer hosted fallback but consider data residency/privacy constraints
[12:29] Jasmine: we'll need to check legal for fallback to hosted, may be blocked for certain flows
[12:34] Alex: noted, add that to next steps for Rohit to confirm allowed routes
[12:39] Priya: quick note on bench design: include both synthetic poisson arrivals and replay of production traces to cover burstiness; do cold-starts and warm-starts to measure KV warmup curves
[12:52] Rohit: we'll share a week of anonymized traffic traces after redaction
[12:56] Samir: what's the expected KV warmup time? we saw minutes to tens of minutes previously
[13:02] Marco: warmup depends on reuse patterns. If you have sticky prefixes it can be sub-5 minutes for high-value flows; for random long-tail it might take hours. Pre-warming by replaying representative traces speeds this up
[13:16] Jasmine: can we pin critical prefixes during deploy to avoid user-facing regressions?
[13:21] Priya: yes pinning is recommended during migrations; remember to unpin after stability checks to recover capacity
[13:28] Alex: ok folks, let's recap next steps and who owns what
[13:33] (brief recap by Alex)
[13:35] Alex: Priya to run bench and share results, Alex to send docs, Rohit to share traces and peering details, Jasmine and Samir to validate security constraints for hosted fallback
[13:46] Jasmine: thanks all, really helpful
[13:48] Priya: thanks everyone, we'll follow up in thread
[13:50] End of transcript
